title: Metzora: the bird set free (Leviticus 14:7)
hookLine: one bird is let go over the open field

cards: A bird trapped in a room panics against the glass. Then someone opens a window, and all at once it finds the gap and it's gone. Silence, and an open sky.

The ritual for coming home from tzara'at has a moment like that. Outside the camp, the priest stands with the person who has been healed, and two small birds, alike. Only one of them will still be there at the end.

teach.b: Why birds at all? Rashi offers an answer: the affliction came from chattering, from careless speech, so the person brings birds, which chirp and twitter all day.
The rite holds up a picture of the very thing that caused the trouble. Then the two fates. One bird is slaughtered over an earthen bowl of fresh running water.
The living bird is dipped, along with the cedar, scarlet and hyssop, and the person is sprinkled seven times.
Then the priest lets the living bird go, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "into the open field."
The Mishnah adds a detail: he doesn't turn toward the sea, or toward the city, or toward the wilderness, but toward the open field, as the verse says. And what does the free bird mean?
The Torah doesn't say, and readers have offered different answers. Some say the impurity is carried off and away.
Some hear the person in the bird: someone shut outside, now released, flying back to life. And some teachers put the two birds side by side. The same kind of speech can wound, or it can sing.
One bird is the old way of talking, ended; the other is the voice set free to start again. All of these are interpretations.
What the text gives is the picture itself: the priest's hands opening, and a small bird climbing over a field.

how: The bird ritual of Leviticus 14 belonged to the Temple era and is not performed today; Jews study it in the weekly Torah reading, and some teachers draw lessons about speech and release from it.

games.q: you're the priest, holding the living bird, dipped and ready. which way do you send it?
games.why: toward the open field, the text says, and the Mishnah adds: not the sea, not a city, not the desert.

practice: Think of something you're holding that has done its time: an old resentment, a story you keep retelling about yourself, a hurt that's already been answered.

Picture it as a small bird in your cupped hands, and notice how tightly you're holding it. On an out-breath, let your hands open and the bird lift toward an open field; you don't have to watch where it goes.
